I think it’s possible to give some written or verbal form to the ideas inherent within a film. I think there’s an underlying thesis within all films but the most brilliant ones could have entire essays written about them. I don’t know how useful it is because you will always lose a great deal of the power of the film by trying to reduce a visual form down to a written one but if I can’t write about it then I either don’t understand what the movie is about or there is no real expression done by the filmmaker. I mean the Batman Begins “controlling idea” that you put forward isn’t wrong as much as it is incomplete. That is a central idea of the film but it lacks all of the context or the complexity within it and gives a reductionist view of the ethical and moral difficulties that the film is centered on so strongly. It’s not that you are wrong, it’s that the mode of interpretation, or rather the brevity of the controlling idea creates a false vision. I find the main thematic underpinnings of the film, and the trilogy in general, to be concerning justice. Batman is a vigilante figure who tries to correct the self destructive and morally chaotic Gotham city outside of the jurisdiction and authority of the democratically elected state. However, the principle antagonist to the film, far more than the destructive organized crime groups like Falcone’s organization, is a radical, fascistic militia group who abandon faith in Gothams ability to organically self correct and decided to organize Gotham’s implosion through hallucinatory chemical weapons. So both parties have the same pursuit, with different means of carrying it out. So in essence boiling it down into the catchphrase “It’s not who you are underneath. It’s what you do that defines you” is true, but that could equally be interpreted as a call to heroism and transcending inaction. But I don’t think that’s the primary concern of the movie, because passivity is not the primary threat to Gotham, it is a threat, but a fanatical devotion to principle is what causes Gothams flirtation with oblivion. So I believe that it is not just possible, but stimulating to analyze films while trying to not over intellectualize the experience and devoid it of its emotional power. I actually think it’s necessary, not to see how smart we are or to come up with a single unchallengeable and un disposable interpretation of a film, but to also defend against propaganda as well. I think the Batman example is a great one because the major cultural fascination and obsession with superheroes and the genres natural sympathies with propaganda and fascist impulses are important to recognize. Superheroes becomes cultural icons and tend to be on the verge of worship, they are usually presented as totally altruistic and completely just, ethical discussion regarding their inherent vigilantism is practically nonexistent, and their antagonists are defeated with relish and encouraged by the audience from their immediate introduction. So examining that dichotomy in a post imperial, modern society is important. But as I said before I don’t want to forget the emotional power of a story, but cinema operates on two separate fields, there is the form of visual storytelling and there is the narrative. The form can be discussed, but in much more general terms, it’s a common saying that a picture is worth a thousand words, but a movie is 24 pictures per second for 2-3 hours. So converting the visual form into words has diminishing returns. But I see no reason why we cannot discuss and write about film narrative like you would a piece of literature. To distill the narrative on screen to a concise, well reasoned and observant piece of criticism that acknowledges the moral and ethical implications of the events and the characters behavior, recognizes the thematic content and tries to find with the film itself and the context of the time and creator of the piece the intent behind the expression. A film like 2001 can’t be reduced down to a single line of written prose, but you can write pages and pages about the ways in which Kubrick focuses on evolution, tribal conflict, artificial intelligence and the questions of the metaphysical in the age of science.

IMHO what is 'easy entertainment' depends upon how much thought the medium stimulates, and also how easily decipherable it is.  For example, I just finished the Brothers Karamazov in audiobook form, I found the language easy to follow even if some of the matters were weighty.  I also listened to the Green Mile, and while that book was less than 1/3 the length of the Dostoevsky tome, I found that it also dealt with weighty matters (even if some of it was supernatural).  Stephen King has a reputation for writing 'easy entertainment' yet I don't think that's fair to his entire body of work.

Movies like Armageddon are most definitely 'easy entertainment' (in fact the less thought one puts into it the more enjoyable the movie is), as was Game of Thrones season 8, which was essentially a non-stop popcorn fest of sex and violence with little to no plot cohesion.  Compare that to Game of Thrones season 1-4, which had intricately crafted scheming and character motivation, and it's IMHO a shame that the series ended on such an 'easy' note.

Just to reiterate, my point is simple, it's not the genre that makes it 'easy', but rather whether or not it stimulates a good amount of thought.

edit - to add another example, Greek dramas tend to be considered 'weighty', yet I remember in high school I read Lysistrata.  That work, while a Greek drama, has more in common with modern pornography than it does with anything 'weighty'.

This is not a very r/TrueFilm kind of movie, but I'm not only going to call it a classic, I'm going to abuse a Pederewski quote for this:

>The greatest accomplishment of any artist in any form of human endeavour whatsoever.

I very recently rewatched this favourite of mine, in hard times, and I was repeatedly astounded by its simple granduer. Many a film - by the likes of Lean, Jackson or Scott - have outdone it for the sheer number of moving parts, but few have matched its emotional honesty, and its focus on visual storytelling.

I feel like when we say "Visual storytelling" we often basically devolve it to montage and painting a mood: so slow motion and drenched colour means sad and that kind of stuff. Braveheart's visual storytelling is not like that: there are sequences of ten to fifteen minutes in a row, where nary a word is spoken, and they're not about trekking montages of setting a mood, but they actually forward the plot.

The directorial choices continually bewilder me. There's a confrontation here between Wallace, the Council and Robert the Bruce, just before the Battle of Falkirk. First thing, Wallace has an entrance as showstopping as anything, partially because Gibson (as the director) has him enter right in the middle of another character giving dialogue. Then, when Wallace goes into a one-on-one discussion with The Bruce, we start with a wideshot in which the nobles are in the shot. Then we punch in closer, but Gibson cunningly keeps the biggest closeup to the most dramatic moment later in the dialogue. Its simple, and its brilliant.

Ontop of all of that, to have this film - which is Gibson's sophomoric directorial effort - be so sure-handed is nothing short of a minor miracle. Its in the pacing: I feel like most directors, given this material, would be a little bit of a rush to get to Stirling. But Gibson isn't: he makes you sit and wait patiently for it. And its not done in a David Lean-like largesse, but just as self-assured: "No, dear audience, this is important, and you will sit hear and enjoy this shot, and now appreciate this beat, and you will wait."

If that's a minor miracle, the pulling off of the battles is as great a miracle as anything described in any biblical tale: that the film didn't implode here defies belief. These battles have been used as a template and inspiration for just about any large-scale ground battle filmed since 1995, but its scarcely if ever been better: the build-up is so drawn-out, it wouldn't feel out of place in a Sergio Leone film, and the combination of staccato cutting, foreground acton, copious gore effects and smart choices of lenses from John Toll all create a most visceral experience.

Performances are uniformally excellent, especially an outstanding, hillarious David O'Hara. The look of the film is gorgeous: Gibson and Toll's decision to NOT wait to magic hours and sunny days gave the film a look that may be less pretty than Gladiator or Ryan's Daughter, but has much more atmosphere: There are movies that take place in icy tundras where you don't feel the cold as palpably as you do here.

And I find the ending incredibly unlifting, moving and glorious: its a cinematic Verklarung. No movie that I've ever seen before or since leaves me with this feeling of walking on air after its over.

To me, terror and horror are not the same.

Terror is typical of short duration.  Horror may be of infinite duration.

Terror is typically localized.  Horror may be cosmic.

Terror is typically psychologically superficial.  Horror is often psychologically deep.

Terror often has an understood basis. Horror often has a basis that cannot be understood--indeed, some horrors don't seem to have a basis, or that basis is unknowable.

The thing causing the terror can often be destroyed, placated, run away from.  The thing causing a horror often cannot be destroyed, cannot be placated or run from.  It subsumes a being or grinds it away.

I could compare a typical Stephen King terror to a typical H.P. Lovecraft or William Hope Hodgson or Clark Ashton Smith horror.

>There was a bursting as of an exploding bladder, a slushy nastiness as of a cloven sunfish, a stench as of a thousand opened graves, and a sound that the chronicler would not put on paper. For an instant the ship was befouled by an acrid and blinding green cloud, and then there was only a venomous seething astern; where—God in heaven!—the scattered plasticity of that nameless sky-spawn was nebulously recombining in its hateful original form, whilst its distance widened every second as the Alert gained impetus from its mounting steam. (from The Call of Cthulhu by Lovecraft)

Notice that most of that description is necessarily indirect because Lovecraft attempts to describe what cannot be described, or if it can be described, is wholly inadequate, even silly in hindsight.  Human words cannot capture a horror; they often fail.  By contrast, it is usually quite easy to describe the cause of a terror.

The character in the Lovecraft story does not write a bladder exploded, but that is the only thing he could compare some unknown aspect of his experience to--not a sound per se.  He does not write it had a specific stench, but that a thousand open graves is the only thing he could imagine he might compare the smell to--and I do not doubt that is hyperbole upon imagination as that character might not know what even one open grave smells like, let alone a thousand.  He does not write the chronicler knew what the sound was, merely that whatever it might have been, the chronicler does not report it.

I.e. there is a void at the center of the description.  The puny statue which a character describes earlier in the story is almost a parody of the real thing.  After all, characters can hold that statute, but no one would want to be in the grip of Cthulhu.

This differs profoundly from e.g. a teenager with special powers (as in Carrie) or a vampire (as in 'Salem's Lot) or any other typical terror.

Well, I'd highly recommend reading what actual film critics -- and not just random people online -- have to say about Kurosawa, or Ozu, or any other big-name director. 

Take the most famous of film critics, the late Roger Ebert. Here's an excerpt from the [obituary](https://www.rogerebert.com/interviews/akira-kurosawa-focused-on-individual-ethical-dilemmas) he wrote when Kurosawa died in 1998:

>He combined two qualities not always found together in filmmakers: He was a visual stylist, and a thoughtful humanist. His films had a daring, exhilarating visual freedom, and a heart of deep human understanding. He often made movies about heroes, but their challenge was not simply to win; it was to make the right ethical choice.

Ebert's [review](https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/great-movie-the-seven-samurai-1954) of *Seven Samurai*, which he identifies as one of the Great Movies, opens with a consideration of the film's influence/historical importance:

>Akira Kurosawa's "Seven Samurai" (1954) is not only a great film in its own right, but the source of a genre that would flow through the rest of the century. The critic Michael Jeck suggests that this was the first film in which a team is assembled to carry out a mission--an idea which gave birth to its direct Hollywood remake, "The Magnificent Seven," as well as "The Guns of Navarone," "The Dirty Dozen" and countless later war, heist and caper movies. Since Kurosawa's samurai adventure "Yojimbo" (1960) was remade as "A Fistful of Dollars" and essentially created the spaghetti Western, and since this movie and Kurosawa's "The Hidden Fortress" inspired George Lucas' "Star Wars" series, it could be argued that this greatest of filmmakers gave employment to action heroes for the next 50 years, just as a fallout from his primary purpose.

A brief analysis of the film's cinematography:

>Kurosawa constantly uses deep focus to follow simultaneous actions in the foreground, middle and background. Often he delineates the distance with barriers. Consider a shot where the samurai, in the foreground, peer out through the slats of a building and across an empty ground to the sight of the bandits, peering in through the slats of a barrier erected against them. Kurosawa's moving camera often avoids cuts in order to make comparisons, as when he will begin on dialogue in a closeup, sweep through a room or a clearing, and end on a closeup of another character who is the point of the dialogue.

The late Donald Richie was, in my opinion, the most perceptive American critic of Japanese cinema. He wrote books about both Ozu and Kurosawa that are well worth reading.

\---

I think the big question is, what exactly is greatness in cinema? How would you define it? Certainly, one aspect (relevant to both Kurosawa and Ozu) is their profound influence on filmmakers across the world.

Eraserhead: creepy, beautiful, not entirely effective. Once we get into the room with the radiator, the film takes off. I prefer my Lynch to start off a bit grounded. Shocked at how impressive and unique the visuals were.

Blade Runner: really really enjoyed it. All time vibe. Mishima: Not really successful, but idc because I love this film. I love the visuals. I love the source material, I love the tone. This is a film that has the right energy even if some of the shorts take a wildly broad tone for the subtle and dark stories from which they are based

I don’t really see the point of setting the movie up like this; the second half is so self-contained narratively and thematically, and so much better than the first half, that it’s never very clear why they bothered including the first half at all. With some massive cuts, this could have been at least a solid comedy, but as is I don’t think I can give it more than a **5/10**.

**Solaris (1972, Andrei Tarkovsky) — re-watch** — I don’t think any other filmmaker has ever rewarded re-watching quite as much and as consistently as Tarkovsky. Tarkovsky’s *Solaris* has often been called a response to, or counterpoint to, *2001: A Space Odyssey*, but I don’t think I fully appreciated how true that is until this viewing.

Both movies are superficially similar in structure, being slow, cerebral science-fiction epics which divide rather neatly into three parts, and they both end on a note which is much stranger and more surreal than the already rather odd rest of the movie. But *2001* conveyed its ideas first and foremost through visual spectacle, and the characters were basically an afterthought; Kubrick suggests that the things revealed to Dave are so much bigger and more beautiful than anything in our ordinary experience that our individual personalities, life stories and relationships come to seem irrelevant when faced with them. But *Solaris*, one of Tarkovsky’s most profoundly humanist works, takes the opposite tack to Kubrick’s borderline nihilism — in this movie, human relationships and emotions seem to be things central to the purpose of the universe; so much so that even the consciousness of a distant planet, once it becomes aware of itself, can’t help but do everything in its power to try to understand them.

Despite being more inclined towards Tarkovsky’s philosophy, I must admit that Kubrick’s movie is the better one. But being as *2001* is, in my opinion, the single greatest movie ever made, so this isn’t saying much. Taken in itself, *Solaris* still holds up as a stunningly beautiful and basically perfect movie. **10/10**

**Solaris (2002, Steven Soderbergh)** — Breaking from chronological order again, and like last time, I decided to pick the most obvious choice. Soderbergh’s 2002 remake of *Solaris* is a divisive movie, and I can see why. Taken on its own terms, it’s a good movie — a compelling and well-written sci-fi drama, though hampered a bit by occasionally clunky exposition. If it were the only film version of this story that existed, it’d be easy to sneer at those who complain about it being slow and dull as philistines. But the thing is, those of us who prefer sci-fi with a slower and more meditative approach already have a perfectly good movie version of *Solaris*, and this version doesn’t really do anything that that didn’t do better. So it’s hard to see what reason there would be for remaking it, unless it’s to be a more easily-accessible version of the story for those who would regard Tarkovsky’s version as too slow and confusing — and if that’s the goal, then it’s a fair point to say that most such viewers will probably not be able to get into this version, either.

So, I can understand why a lot of people dislike this version of the story. But that doesn’t mean I agree. Because, taking it on its own terms, it is still a pretty good movie. Recommended. **7/10**

**Cries and Whispers (1972, Ingmar Bergman) — re-watch** — What do you think of when you think of the colour red? Ingmar Bergman said that he thought of red as the colour of the soul. Whether or not he was right about, the more obvious association, at least to me, is that it’s the colour of blood. It’s also the colour of fire; but perhaps most importantly, it is, in a less literal but equally obvious sense, the colour of heat and passion.

I bring this up because *Cries and Whispers* is famously, and literally, an extremely red movie. Not only are almost all of the sets mostly red, and often with additional red objects prominently featured as props, but even the scene transitions use fades to red instead of black. It might seem unusual to view a particular colour as key to a film’s appeal, but I really don’t think the film would be anywhere near as effective as it is if a different colour had featured so prominently instead, or if no colour had. *Cries and Whispers* is a harrowing experience to sit through. It’s the coldest and saddest movie Bergman ever put out, which is saying a lot considering that Bergman is known primarily for having made so many of the most bitterly cold and crushingly depressing movies ever made. The levels of cynicism it delves to could very easily make it totally unbearable, if the environment and even the filmmaking itself did not seem to be in an almost active revolt against it, bursting with the colours of the passions that its human characters refuse to show. The contrast makes for one of the most stunning and unforgettable moviegoing experiences of all time. Another basically perfect movie. **10/10**

What’s fascinating about *Come and See* is that it almost weaponizes the absence of craft you mention. The lack of rhythm, payoff, or catharsis isn’t a failure of storytelling - it’s an intentional refusal. Made in the mid-80s, it arrives at a time when the Soviet Union was beginning to rethink its own war mythology. In that sense, the “incompleteness” isn’t a flaw but part of the film’s historical position: it’s cinema refusing to give its audience a traditional narrative to hide inside.

When you compare it to something like *Grave of the Fireflies*, which is devastating because of its emotional rhythm, or *Shoah*, which devastates through duration and testimony, *Come and See* feels like it’s working in a third register: a purely sensory destabilization. The sound design, the distortions of perspective, even the actor’s gaze into the camera - they collapse the safe distance that most films maintain.

I think that’s why people call it a masterpiece. Not because it’s “enjoyable,” or even narratively satisfying, but because it dares to ask whether cinema can serve as testimony rather than story.

So maybe the real question isn’t “is it good cinema?” but “what do we want cinema to do?” Should it console us with craft, or disturb us with witness?

To more directly answer your question though, I think that, in theory, yes, if we lived lives without great stress, we wouldn't rely so much on this extreme escapism, however, I wouldn't really blame that stress on global problems. I've always viewed boredom as the gradual bubbling up of suppressed emotions during the quiet hours when there're fewer distractions to keep them at bay. That's why boredom always comes with a sense of unease, where we seek out distractions for comfort.

Buddhist meditation for example, is "structured boredom", where you not only trigger the unease, but amplify them through focus, in order to get to their roots. For a seasoned meditator, it's entirely normal to experience the mundane without the unease that comes with boredom, or at least the unease doesn't "get to her" as much.

In the absence of unease, there's less need for distractions, and therefore less demand for the type of escapism that seeks to stimulate the senses. But I think there are more subtle forms of escapism.

Speaking of which, I see economic and political malaise as important, though not sole contributors to people's collective mental health, and therefore popularity of escapism. For example, the wide acceptance of income inequality and free will in modern capitalism on the one hand can seem rather liberating for those who are able to catch the waves. But for those who fall behind despite the apparent presence of opportunities, life can seem especially debilitating, because any failure is more attributed to her own doings, and less to external circumstances. 

This leads to two popular types of subtle escapism in film: 1) the hero who overcomes extraordinary odds through her own power (for those who ride the wave but not at the top, the allure is an escape to the top), and 2) the hero who overcomes extraordinary odds through divine intervention (for those who feel left behind). Neither of these portray the protagonist coping with failures, which is the far more likely outcome given extraordinary odds. It's not he nature of the messages themselves, but rather the imbalance in portrayal of outcomes that's particularly nefarious when it comes to setting expectations.

On the other hand, there are plenty of escapist movies that are still plenty talked about years after their release. Singin' in the Rain is pretty much pure escapism, and yet decades later it is still often revered as one of the greatest films ever made. Just because something is escapist doesn't mean it isn't a serious or great film.

While everyone has their own tastes and their subjective take on whether a movie is "good" or "bad" is always valid, there are objective ways to measure the quality of a movie: whether it communicates its message effectively, whether it has elements that don't accomplish what they're supposed to or take the audience out of the moment or are simply distracting, whether the story flows properly and explains everything that needs explaining, etc. When using this more objective definition, I prefer the term "failed" movies, because that's what they are: movies that failed to communicate what they set out to communicate for whatever reasons.

With that in mind, there are lots of reasons to enjoy failed art. The most obvious is that they're often accidentally funny in their failure, because comedy that wasn't intended to be comedy is still entertaining to watch and because there's something satisfying about an artist swinging for the fences as hard as they can and coming nowhere near close to hitting the ball. There's also a lot of value in failed movies for people who understand and appreciate the mechanics of film as a medium and can benefit from seeing what happens when things are done incorrectly and asking what could be improved. Failed movies also tend to be daring, failing because they decided to try something really new and challenging instead of making a safe, derivative movie and it just didn't come together like they'd hoped, and those movies often have kernels of really interesting ideas that you just wouldn't find in any other movie and that you can see how they might have been great if certain decisions were made differently. And of course there is the appeal of kitsch, of liking something regardless of its "objective" quality just because you like it and you enjoy liking it and sharing that enjoyment with others who like it.

I guess the TL;DR is that failed movies often (I'd argue always) have *some* value as works of art, whether they're accidental comedy or a cautionary tale or an exploration of how the mechanics of film fail sometimes. I think that we should all strive to ask ourselves, when we see a film that is "bad", exactly why it is bad and maybe even why parts of it are good or enjoyable despite that. I know ever since I decided to do that, I've started liking all movies a lot more.

Well, in the same way that science is the exploration of objective reality, art is the exploration of subjective reality. Language is useful but it’s an ultimately clumsy technology that’s incapable of fully translating complex inner experience to others. Art is our best tool to for this exact task.
